entities.name: Saint Sava
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Sava (born Rastko Nemanjić, c. 1171 – 1236-01-21) stands as a foundational figure in Serbian history, theology, and national identity. A Serbian prince and the youngest son of Stefan Nemanja, the founder of the Nemanjić dynasty and the medieval Serbian state, Sava renounced his royal inheritance for monasticism on Mount Athos. His pivotal role as the first Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church, established in 1219, irrevocably shaped the spiritual, cultural, and political landscape of medieval Serbia and its enduring legacy.

After his monastic vows on Mount Athos, where he founded Hilandar Monastery with his father, Sava returned to Serbia and embarked on a monumental organizational and diplomatic mission. In 1219, he successfully negotiated the autocephaly (ecclesiastical independence) of the Serbian Church from the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, a crucial step in solidifying Serbian statehood under his brother Stefan the First-Crowned. Sava then meticulously organized the new church, establishing dioceses, consecrating bishops, and compiling the Krmčija (Nomocanon of Saint Sava), a comprehensive legal code blending ecclesiastical canons with Byzantine civil law, which became the bedrock of Serbian law for centuries.

Saint Sava's legacy extends far beyond his ecclesiastical and legal reforms. He fostered a distinct Serbian cultural and educational identity, promoting literacy, church building, and monastic scholarship. His travels to the Holy Land and his diplomatic efforts also enhanced Serbia's standing in the Orthodox world. His work laid the spiritual and institutional groundwork for the powerful Serbian Empire that would emerge in the 14th century, ensuring the Serbian Orthodox Church's integral role in national life, a bond that persists to this day.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saint Sava's establishment of an independent Serbian Orthodox Church and his legal and cultural reforms laid the spiritual and institutional foundations for medieval Serbian statehood and profoundly shaped Serbian national identity, influencing an entire nation's trajectory for centuries.
